HEADLINE: Why free-to-air TV is still king in advertising
TEXT:
Marketers have backed one of the key drivers behind Nine's takeover of Fairfax Media: the ongoing lure of advertising on free-to-air TV, even as viewers move to streaming services.

While advertising in newspapers continues to rapidly decline, free-to-air TV is bucking the trend, with major corporations saying it still makes up a critical part of their marketing strategy.

Standard Media Index figures for 2017 revealed that advertising spend across newspapers was down 22.3 per cent and 20.8 per cent for magazines, while television avoided the landslide, slipping only 0.7 per cent across the calendar year. The Australian Financial Review was the only paper in 2017 to grow print advertising revenue, and print and digital readership were up 15 per cent and 40 per cent respectively.

Telstra general manager of media and sponsorships, Genelle Sharples, said free-to-air advertising was the cornerstone of the telco's advertising strategy.

"In a highly fragmented media environment, free-to-air TV consistently delivers higher audience reach than any other single medium," Ms Sharples told The Australian Financial Review.

"We're highly selective about when and where we advertise and prioritise major sporting moments such as NRL, AFL and netball games, news and current affairs and the most popular drama and special event series."

In February, figures from KPMG on television advertising revenue revealed that for the first time in 13 years Nine Entertainment had come out on top with the largest share of advertising dollars for the 2017 calendar year.

Nine's share of the market increased to 38.3 per cent, while Seven and Ten had 37.9 per cent and 23.8 per cent respectively. Nine's momentum looked set to continue, with its lead extending to 40 per cent of the market for the second half of 2017. The network's strong performance is also likely to lift another notch thanks to the announcement last week that Nine and Fairfax Media had agreed to a merger, which will result in Nine having a controlling 51.1 per cent stake.

Nine group content strategy director Lizzie Young said that, if the merger was given the green light, it would give the network an additional advertising revenue boost.

"Assuming it goes the way we would like, there are two big benefits. We've been doing all this work to leverage our content brands [like The Block or Married at First Sight] across broadcast video on demand (BVOD) and social media and more, and it can be extrapolated even further with Fairfax's assets and platforms." she said.

"We will end up with this suite of products for clients, which is an amazing platform. At a content strategy level there will also be opportunities. The Block and Domain are already in a partnership, but we can think about beyond that what else we can do."

Founder of marketing consultancy Marketing Angels, Michelle Gamble, said that, when it came to driving recall and attracting new customers, TV was king for brands.

"Potential customers are 53 per cent as likely to recall television ads as existing customers compared to 41 per cent for mobile advertising. This was a stat we recently sourced from Zenith Touchpoints ROI Tracker as part of our own social media," she said.

"The rise of ad-blocking technology and usage means that other digital channels (particularly YouTube) will struggle to gain market share and spend directly from TV."

Ms Young said Nine's performance recently was the result of two years of hard work in which it reinvigorated its content and invested in building content brands around its program, which could be leveraged beyond 30-second free-to-air TV advertisements via things like program sponsorships.

The network had also been experimenting with social media and was in conversations with YouTube and Google. "It's well documented that we spend a large sum of money creating this content, and then putting into these new platforms is very difficult to monetise. Love Island content had 170 million streams on YouTube, but very little revenue in return," Ms Young said.

Like Telstra, TV advertising continues to be a key component of gambling company Tabcorp's multi-channel marketing strategy. General manager of marketing for its lotteries and keno business, Andrew Shepherd, said it was a cost-effective communications channel that delivered strong mainstream reach. "[It delivers an] emotional connection and retail call to action for our brands," he said.

Ms Sharples said that, while free-to-air advertising was the cornerstone of Telstra's marketing strategy, its spending had shifted over the last few years to be more targeted about when and where its advertising appears.

"Free-to-air TV networks are largely the masters of their own destiny because their commercial success or failure depends on their ability to provide advertisers with an efficient and cost-effective means of reaching particular audiences, by location, demographic and personal preferences - and that comes down to the quality of the television they produce," she said.

Network Ten executive general manager of revenue and client partnerships Rod Prosser admitted that the station, which was acquired by US company CBS last year, had had a tumultuous few years and was playing catch-up in terms of the data analytics it was able to provide to advertisers, but was investing heavily in this strategy.

He said 2018 had been a good year for TV advertising across the industry so far with many major sporting events like the Winter Olympics and Commonwealth Games.

Network Ten had not been the broadcaster of any of these, but he said the network was positioned for a stronger second half off the back of the success of programs like Masterchef, which has helped it narrow the ratings gap with Nine and Seven.

"Generally there's been a readjustment from clients that had been over-indexing in digital. There are clients that won't advertise on social media now because they know it's not brand safe and they don't know that their ad won't fall around content that's inappropriate for the brand. We offer a brand safe environment for advertisers, along with mass reach and a diversified business."

We will end up with this suite of products for clients, which is an amazing platform. Lizzie Young, group content strategy director, Nine Entertainment

HEADLINE: Getting on board: Outdoor advertising's manic week of global deal-making
TEXT:
Inside the deal Four CEOs in three countries pulled off two big wins.

As Danielle Decaux celebrated her 80th birthday, she watched her son Jean-François, now co-chief executive of the French outdoor advertising giant she and her late husband Jean-Claude built, pursue one of the biggest transaction's in the company's history. And it was all the way on the other side of the globe.

JCDecaux's $1.2 billion deal to buy Australia's APN Outdoor capped off a manic week in the outdoor advertising sector. Here, There & Everywhere's Adshel was also in play, meaning there were four chief executives in three different countries hashing out negotiations to crunch a deal.

"It was probably the best birthday present I could give to my mother," Jean-François told the The Australian Financial Review.

"They both started the company. My father was a bill poster, and my mother was helping him to stick paper posters on billboards. They built the company together. When I was able to announce the transaction had been approved by the board she was delighted."

All understand the deals aren't over the line yet. The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission is set to pour over JCDecaux's takeover of APN Outdoor as well as oOh!media's $570 million acquisition of Adshel.

JCDecaux is no stranger to the Australian market. It chose an organic growth path after establishing a presence ahead of the 2000 Sydney Olympics. That didn't mean it didn't take the odd glance - it ran the ruler over APN Outdoor in 2014 before it listed. But four years later, it could no longer afford to ignore consolidation in Australia's outdoor advertising sector or a chance to get into the billboard market, dominated by APN Outdoor and oOh!media.

JCDecaux, APN Outdoor, oOh!media and Adshel are the four largest players in the Australian out-of-home advertising sector. The outdoor sector makes up just 6.1 per cent, or about $1 billion, of the total advertising pie in Australia of about $17.3 billion, according to PricewaterhouseCoopers.

In Europe, JCDecaux enlisted Goldman Sachs chairman of investment banking François-Xavier de Mallmann, commonly known as FX. In Australia, Goldman Sachs head of investment banking services Zac Fletcher, head of technology, media and telecommunications Adrian Lee and Sydney-based Herbert Smith Freehills partner Rebecca Maslen-Stannage were on board.

After it became clear Adshel was on the block and APN Outdoor was running hard at it with a bid in late May, JCDecaux needed to act quickly. It assembled its bid team and began work on Project Opera.

For his own run at Adshel, and his quick pivot to engage with JCDecaux, APN Outdoor chief executive James Warburton would enlist long-time advisers Cadence Advisory managing director Garren Cronin and associate director Tom Stevens, Allens partners Tom Story and Julian Donnan. Later Morgan Stanley's Robert Mete and Luke Boeg would also be drafted in to what was dubbed Project Torch.

Warburton had returned to the media sector with APN Outdoor on January 22 following a four-year stint at Archer Capital's V8 Supercars.

The former Network Ten boss and senior Seven West Media executive made clear he wanted to make a big impact in the outdoor sector by building up APN Outdoor. The company had struggled without a CEO for much of 2017 after the exit of long-time boss Richard Herring in September 2017. Herring's departure originally was due to a planned merger with rival oOh!media but he continued out the door even when that deal was nixed.

Warburton was candid about the company's need to do better when he took the job. APN Outdoor upgraded its guidance in May, following contract wins and renewals, and its shares were up nearly 40 per cent in the three months before JCDecaux's approach.

"It's real credit to the APN team," Warburton said on June 26 after the deal was agreed. "There are a lot of good people here, they don't lose their ability, they just lose their confidence, it's just been about putting it back."

When APN Outdoor presented to JCDecaux late on Friday, June 22, oOh!media chief executive Brendon Cook was at lunch in London with his son, daughter-in-law and grandson, taking calls as his team in Sydney went through the final contracts on his long sought-after deal to buy Adshel, known internally as Project Hyperion.

Cook founded oOh!media, then known as Outdoor Network Australia, in 1989 and has made the company one of the driving forces of consolidation in the sector, as well as comfortably more than doubling its share price since its second float in 2014. It was previously acquired and delisted in 2012 by Champ Private Equity. Cook had long coveted Adshel. Street furniture was one of the missing pieces for oOh!media when Cook and his executive team drew up a plan of where they should expand the business in 2011.

However, Adshel and JCDecaux, who have the lion's share of the street furniture segment of outdoor advertising, had both not been for sale given their ownership structures.

That all changed in 2016, when HT&E, then known as APN News & Media, bought out the 50 per cent of Adshel it didn't already own for $268 million from its international partner Clear Channel Outdoor Holdings.

HT&E CEO Ciaran Davis has spent his tenure scaling back the business. The Irishman, who came to Australia in 2010 as chief executive of Australian Radio Network, reshaped HT&E's earnings profile, drastically reducing its exposure to declining areas such as print, which made up 60 per cent of revenue four years ago, exiting regional newspapers and spinning off its New Zealand business, NZME, to focus on the growth areas of outdoor, radio and digital.

Cook and his team believed Adshel was a more valuable asset than the market was giving HT&E credit for, even after it lost the Yarra Trams contract to JCDecaux. He believed the business would at some point be an acquisition candidate.

oOh!media and HT&E began informal talks six months before the first official approach for Adshel in April. For HT&E it was the starting gun that would kick off Project Valette - the company was happy to hold onto Adshel but if the right price came it was on the table. "We thought that's a sector we'd like to play in. We started talking to Adshel some time ago to see if there was any interest," Cook said on June 25.

Advising Cook was Macquarie Capital's Darren Keogh and Minter Ellison partners Con Boulougouris and Christopher Allen, while in HT&E's corner were Credit Suisse Australia chief executive John Knox, CSLA's head of corporate finance and capital markets Mark Dorney and Bakers McKenzie partner David Holland.

HT&E rejected oOh!media's first approach in April, believed to be about $450 million, as undervaluing Adshel. It wouldn't be long before oOh!media returned with an improved $470 million bid in late May. But, APN Outdoor was moving quickly with a $500 million offer.

HT&E would run an official process with bids due Friday, June 22. Within two days of the looming deadline JCDecaux made its move, lobbing a $1.1 billion bid for APN Outdoor, which had been working hard on an all-cash offer for Adshel, even tapping Morgan Stanley and UBS for a $250 million to $300 million capital raise to fund a prospective offer. One of the conditions for JCDecaux's bid was APN Outdoor not proceed with a takeover of Adshel.

APN Outdoor knew it couldn't be out raising capital for an all-cash bid for Adshel with JCDecaux lurking. But it also didn't want rival oOh!media to get Adshel for a steal. The Australian company's board also knew it needed to engage with JCDecaux because there was potential for a deal that could greatly benefit shareholders.

APN Outdoor would throw in a bid of $540 million for Adshel the morning offers were due, made up of $230 million in cash and $310 million in shares. APN Outdoor made its bid public, meaning it knew oOh!media would know exactly where it needed to get to, but it wouldn't come cheap. HT&E would publicly value the bid at $585 million.

HT&E took final bids at 6pm on Friday, June 22, and oOh!media's advisers Macquarie worked quickly to pre-negotiate and agree to commercial terms early on in the evening.

With Cook on call in London, the next 12 hours were spent finetuning as oOh!media's chief financial officer Sheila Lines, group commercial finance director Chris Roberts and general counsel Maria Polczynski, finalised the deal with HT&E chief financial officer Jeff Howard, with Davis on call, and the two sides' lawyers and financial advisers jumping in and out of Ubers, going between firms, all night. At 8am on Saturday morning they signed contracts for oOh!media to buy Adshel for $570 million.

The potential deal, which will see oOh!media finally entering the street furniture segment, has Cook excited, while HT&E was ecstatic with the price, more than $100 million above the second approach made in May. "We've demonstrated, if somebody wants to come in, we'll drive the best interest of shareholders," Davis said on June 25.

By this time, things were well and truly moving between JCDecaux and APN Outdoor. At 10pm Friday night Warburton and APN Outdoor chief operating officer Andrew Hines were at Goldman Sachs in Sydney giving a presentation to Decaux and his management via video conference to the investment bank's Paris office.

Over the next four days, Warburton, Hines, APN Outdoor chief financial officer Philip Knox, finance general manager David Watkins and their advisers barely left Pyrmont, staying awake all hours as they negotiated with the French giant.

Management and advisers from JCDecaux and APN Outdoor pulled multiple all-nighters, with time zones between Australia and France meaning somebody was working on the deal at all hours of the day. JCDecaux knew they didn't have to rush a deal with the Adshel process settled, but there was genuine desire from the French to do a deal.

APN Outdoor had been sprinting for almost three weeks, having run hard at Adshel up to Friday then continuing on as JCDecaux entered late in that process. On the fourth night of around-the-clock negotiations, the pair agreed to a $1.2 billion deal that was recommended by the APN Outdoor board - both parties walked away happy with the outcome.

Approval from the competition regulator is still pending and the ACCC's ruling is not being taken for granted - a provisional decision date has been set for August 30 on both transactions.

There has been no big party or celebration, just getting back to business, while a bit sleep deprived, following a whirlwind week of deal making.

C'est la vie, as the French say.

It was probably the best birthday present I could give to my mother. Jean-François Decaux, co-chief executive, JCDecaux

HEADLINE: Broadcasters collaborate on briefing portal
TEXT:
Australia's free-to-air and pay television broadcasters have tapped advisory firm IBB Consulting to help find a technology vendor to build a centralised briefing portal.

Nine Entertainment, Seven West Media, Network Ten, Foxtel and Multi-Channel Network have come together, via industry body ThinkTV, to create a new briefing portal which plugs in all their trading platforms to allow advertisers and agencies to brief the broadcasters on a campaign in a single location.

The portal will eliminate the need to repeatedly brief each broadcaster.

The project is seen as the opening gambit by Australia broadcasters to make it easier for advertisers to buy TV advertising and could lead to greater collaboration. The portal is not a centralised ad trading platform and each network will still operate their own system. The portal will act as a gateway for advertisers and agencies to brief and then connect with the broadcaster's various trading platforms; Nine's 9Galaxy, Seven's Code7 and MCN's Landmark, which runs ad trading for Foxtel and Ten.

Initial development of the portal will be narrowly focused so a product can be taken to market as soon as possible. However, that will only be the first stage of development and it is expected the technology will expand and broaden the portal's capabilities.

IBB, which was bought by Accenture in 2017, has taken a detailed request for proposal to selected vendors who will respond in the third quarter to the ThinkTV board of directors. Technology company IPONWEB is believed to be one of the frontrunners.

"This solution will deliver scale and work flow efficiencies for advertisers, agencies and broadcasters and work has begun in earnest to deliver it. It is a complex project and we are consulting media agencies and advertisers to ensure it meets their needs," ThinkTV chief executive Kim Portrate said.

Nine chief sales officer Michael Stephenson said the industry is focused on making TV easier to buy.

"The briefing portal will make the process of briefing and buying TV simpler as it integrates into our systems driving greater efficiency for our clients. This is a great first step with more to come."

Seven chief revenue officer Kurt Burnette said collaboration among sectors is growing as a key factor to future success.

"The ThinkTV briefing portal very much goes to that idea and highlights the real and meaningful collaboration that is happening and will continue to occur for TV and Total Video in this country," he said.

New MCN chief executive Mark Frain said the broadcasters have listened to one of the key pieces of feedback it has got from the market.

"The new briefing portal is the first step on this journey. It will provide agencies and clients a single location for all TV briefs which will increase efficiency, save time and ease the transactional barriers for the whole TV buying marketplace," he said.

Network Ten executive general manager of revenue and client partnerships Rod Prosser said the portal is an example of what the industry can achieve by working together.

It comes as publishing rivals Fairfax Media, publisher of The Australian Financial Review, and News Corp, reached a landmark agreement last week to share printing network resources.

Key pointsAdvertisers will be able to brief on campaigns in a single location.

The developers are aiming to take a product to market as soon as possible.

HEADLINE: Keep calm and measure your level of influence on the world
TEXT:
I am becoming more and more disillusioned with my own tribe.

Does opinion really have so much currency that even academics, in their rush to be noticed, forget to deliver knowledge.

Opinion doesn't give us standards, nor does it give us anything to base them on. We used to learn this in PhD school. There was a time when you could bet your house on everything your professor would say, knowing every word that came out of their mouth was considered and evidence-based. Sure, hypotheses can be disproven, but increasingly opinion is rife, and worse being traded upon. Do you think Professor Stephen Hawking ever traded on opinion?

This brings me to the irony of the moment. Influencer marketing is being publicly vilified by those who are themselves social influencers. And social media is being blasted as having no impact by those who use such platforms as the means of growing their influence. Don't get me wrong, I of all people understand the true and significant differences in advertising effectiveness across TV and online platforms (from our own work considering the impact of TV), but that doesn't mean these platforms don't work at all. And I am not aware of one academic who uses TV to promote their institutes and consultancies.

Earlier in my career a professor criticised my work in understanding the impact of new media because, according to this person, Facebook (and other social platforms) was a fad. I must Google how long a fad typically goes for; my guess is less than 14 years. I have never forgotten this throwaway comment, not just for its short-sightedness but for its lack of curiosity about the massive changes taking place in business, lifestyle and media.

In a way this is how I feel about influencer marketing at the moment. It doesn't go away if we ignore it or call it names. We need to understand it and, more importantly, its relative position in the media mix. Like all things you don't understand at first, you need to dig a little deeper and make an attempt. It's called research.

We are building an Instagram portal to add to our technology that collects attention and sales impact from a viewer. Working with global brands and their agencies we are about to embark on a large-scale UK and Japanese-based study considering the impact of the influencer/follower relationship. Until this study is done I have no comment on its effectiveness.

Calling influencer marketing a flash in the pan, however, is nothing compared to suggestions, by academics who should know better, that artificial intelligence doesn't exist. Yes, it happens. The people who do it publicly are over there in the corner signing a collaboration agreement with the Flat Earth Institute.

My point is the same: as an academic is it really enough to shout your opinion that something doesn't exist? How did you arrive at that opinion? And let's not forget that it is an opinion, we wouldn't want it masquerading as a fact due to its influential source. Is not understanding something the same as it not existing?

I work with Professor Anton van den Hengel of University of Adelaide, an incredibly intelligent person who, just quietly, would never get a job at the Flat Earth Institute. He is the director of the Australian Institute of Machine Learning, has worked with the likes of Microsoft, Facebook, Samsung, Canon.

He has 10 commercialised patents and his work on visual matching is pioneering. Oh, and then there is his number 1 and 2 global ranking in Scene Parsing (a computer vision term for image recognition) and Visual Question Answering (I am told akin to Turin) where the likes of Google compete. Let's ask him if AI exists. Although you probably don't even know who he is, he is not an influencer on social.

Is ignorance a valid reason to dismiss a new idea? At least measure its worth before diminishing its value.

So please learned people, do our industry a favour, tone the language down and act like academics not celebrities. And here's to hoping we do see an impact in our influencer work, because if the power of the influencer doesn't exist then all of our careers as academics bearing influence are over.

Dr Karen Nelson-Field is a professor at University of Adelaide.

Is it really enough to shout your opinion that something doesn't exist?

HEADLINE: Ten unveils Pilot Week line-up
TEXT:
Network Ten has unveiled its line-up for next month's pilot week with a mix of old and new faces, as the CBS-owned free-to-air broadcaster experiments with a number of new formats in search of programming it will commission for a full season.

The eight-show line-up, a number of which have already been leaked - including Trial by Kyle with Kyle Sandilands, Disgrace! with Sam Dastyari, and Taboo - is heavily weighted to comedy and will trial new formats, existing overseas formats, big production house content as well as smaller producers.

Pilot Week will see Ten run a number of new shows during one week before it decides which to commission for a full season.

Other shows include an Australian version of US Comedy Central hit Drunk History, Bring Back Saturday Night (a music and comedy variety show with Rove McManus), Kinne Tonight with comedian Troy Kinne, Dave with Dave O'Neil and Ten's first sketch comedy show in 12 years, Skit Happens.

"The reason for pilot week is we want to invest more in Australian content," Ten chief content officer Beverley McGarvey said.

"We also want to do things that are different. Putting pilots to air and letting the audience have a bit more input is something we're excited to see."

Ten will gauge feedback from audiences who can engage via tenplay and social media. It will also take ratings into account, and different statistics around that, including how many viewers a show keeps from the previous program and whether or not it builds over the episode.

"We would love to be able to keep doing it. It brings out new ideas," Ms McGarvey said.

Omnicom Media Group chief executive of Australia and New Zealand Peter Horgan said the Pilot Week concept was innovative and disruptive.

"I think Ten's role in the free-to-air space has always been to have a crack," he said.

"The cricket was a blow, when you're looking to rebuild, you got to throw some options to viewers. I think clustering that is a good way to make an audience sit up and take notice."

Ten is attempting to go back to its roots with Pilot Week, and build up shows for younger audiences which its rivals Nine and Seven are unlikely to commission.

Being now owned by CBS gives Ten a level of financial security it hasn't had for the best part of a decade, but the US network wants its new Australian business to stand on its own two feet.

It's a tough landscape and being the smallest metropolitan free-to-air broadcaster means every revenue share point is vital.

Network Ten executive general manager of revenue and client partnerships Rod Prosser said the response from advertisers and agencies has been positive.

"It goes back to innovation and it's what Ten has done in the past," he said.

"I think the sponsors aren't looking at it as show specific, they're looking at what they can do across the week."

We want to invest more in Australian content. Beverley McGarvey, Ten chief content officer

HEADLINE: Life's a stream as Netflix and Stan lead on-demand growth
TEXT:
The value of Stan in the Nine takeover of Fairfax has been underscored by new research showing the number of Australians paying for video streaming services has grown by more than 50 per cent in the last year.

Local subscriber numbers to subscription video on demand (SVOD) services such as Netflix and Stan rose 54 per cent to 9.1 million.

While Netflix, in particular, and Stan - which remains 50-50 owned by Fairfax Media, publisher of The Australian Financial Review, and Nine Entertainment until the tie-up is finalised - have had impressive years, research firm Telsyte found Australians were also starting to seriously adopt sports streaming services from telecommunications companies Telstra and Optus.

The research firm compiles its figures from a combination of online surveys with viewers, interviews with executives from service providers, network operators, content providers, retailers, and hardware manufacturers and streaming company reports.

The findings show while pay TV numbers have remained reasonably steady in the past year, Australians are becoming increasingly comfortable with multiple subscription offerings in the VOD market, and are subscribing to multiple providers for distinct offerings, including original content and live sports.

Telsyte estimates Netflix had about 3.9 million Australian subscribers with Stan passing the 1 million mark at the end of June, and remaining the second-largest single service.

Telsyte estimated 43 per cent of Australian households subscribed to SVOD services at the end of June 2018, up from about 30 per cent a year ago. This compares with roughly 70 per cent in the US and 60 per cent in the UK.

Mr Fadaghi said the rapid adoption showed the growth potential of Australia reaching similar levels in a short time. Telsyte believed Netflix and Stan would retain the two top streaming spots in Australia until at least 2020.

Amazon's Prime Video streaming service has so far failed to make much headway in the Australian market, according to Telsyte, but Mr Fadaghi said it would take off eventually if Amazon's companion retail services improved in Australia.

"Amazon is a little late to market, which has limited its ability to license content for Australia exclusively, and has limited original content, making it less attractive to consumers from a entertainment perspective," he said.

"However, when tied into other services, such as delivery, Alexa and e-books it becomes more compelling for consumers. Prime should start to take off similar to the USA when delivery times come down on Prime Delivery."

Telsyte's report said the rollout of the national broadband network in metropolitan areas and availability of 5G mobile networks by 2020 meant high-definition 4k streaming would increasingly become popular.

Bundled sports coverage with mobile phone deals is also increasingly popular, with Telstra's AFL, NRL and Netball Live exceeding 1.5 million users at the end of June 18.

Perhaps surprisingly, it found more than 2 million Australians tuned in to the FIFA World Cup in June via Optus Sport, despite its well-publicised technical problems that led it to give up exclusive rights and simulcast matches on SBS.

Optus has so far declined to say how many people have subscribed to its Optus Sport coverage, but Telsyte said the World Cup had shown that large-scale big sporting events would continue to create demand and opportunities for SVOD service providers.

Telsyte managing director Foad Fadaghi said Optus' technical problems would likely be a short-term problem and its figures showed consumers were starting to embrace the piecemeal nature of on-demand services.

"As we have seen with other carriers, the damage [from technical problems] can be mitigated with the issues being resolved over time. It should be a wake-up call for Optus, which should result in improvements to its customers going forward," Mr Fadaghi said.

"Consumers are ... diversifying their subscriptions to as wide as their interest, spanning TV, movies, children's content and sports, with trial periods, low entry price points and the ability to cancel being drivers."

By comparison to the SVOD numbers, Telsyte found about a third of households subscribed to pay TV at the end of June, which was similar to 2017.

However, Foxtel has been under pressure because of the increasing adoption of SVOD, including its own Foxtel Now service.

Telsyte said its pay TV market measurements, which included cable, satellite and IPTV service Fetch TV, had remained flat despite Foxtel's decline, due to growth in Fetch TV subscriptions via internet providers.

Australians are becoming comfortable with multiple subscription offerings.

HEADLINE: CMOs need a boardroom voice as scrutiny on marketing grows
TEXT:
One could argue that the importance of marketing in the boardroom has never been more critical, as regulators from the European Union, the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), and the ACCC on our own shores all shine the spotlight on aspects of the $700-billion-plus global media and marketing supply chain.

The EU's storm around General Data Protection Regulation privacy legislation has rightfully coupled governance and compliance more closely to the broader marketing growth agenda, and recent headlines that the FBI is circling media trading and transparency practices in the US advertising market is another signal that marketing's role should escalate at board level.

Not only is the chief marketing officer the most important "voice of the customer" and driver of business growth, the expanding remit increasingly impacts on company risk and business performance.

The FBI, the law enforcement arm of the Department of Justice (DoJ), investigates corporate fraud and white-collar crime, including "illicit transactions designed to evade regulatory oversight" and "kickbacks".

The FBI is hunting for a possible rat in the US advertising system. One would assume any such investigation could potentially hold agencies, advertisers and media owners complicit.

This isn't the first time the DoJ has had the advertising industry in its sights. An investigation is still under way on bid rigging in TV and video commercial production contracts. Price-fixing and bid-rigging are prohibited under US federal antitrust law. People could go to prison.

In this US context and with rising global scrutiny on marketing activities and the surrounding ecosystem, two seminal speeches in the past two years by Marc Pritchard, Chief Brand Officer at P&G, should be revisited with more veracity. With a $7 billion advertising budget, P&G is the world's largest corporate spender on advertising and marketing.

Both Pritchard's groundbreaking speeches were delivered as chairman of the Association of National Advertisers (ANA) in the US, the same industry group that triggered intense global industry debate by commissioning an investigation into media rebates, advertising arbitrage, trading and transparency around media buying practices. That was in 2016.

In February 2017, Pritchard put marketers "on notice", challenging them to probe deeper into the "murky" media supply chain and reclaim marketing as the stimulus for business growth.

Exactly one year later, with the backing of 1000 CMOs from the ANA in the US, Pritchard implored marketers to take back control of a marketing system from external partners and suppliers, to whom they had divested too much responsibility.

"This is the year we take back control to transform the industry through mass disruption," Pritchard said, compelling marketers with his new, equally ambitious agenda to "reinvent media, reinvent advertising and reinvent agency partnerships".

When P&G speaks, the marketing industry listens and indeed, research from the World Federation of Advertisers has found that three-quarters of major multinational advertisers are reviewing their current agency partnerships, looking at whether they have the right mix of agencies and capabilities from external partners.

So what will Pritchard's next instalment in February 2019 be?

My guess: a call to arms for more sophisticated marketing and media attribution interrogation - that is, both predictive tech and robust post-analysis on which marketing investments are doing the heavy lifting for business growth. Algorithms are on the rise to calibrate media investments focused on short- and mid-range sales outcomes rather than audience delivery.

The priority must now be on building out the final proof point of marketing's effectiveness to legitimise its right to the boardroom agenda for delivering sustainable growth without waste.

Marketing's efficacy has never been as important or as complicated as it is today, and if past form is a guide, Pritchard and P&G will have a solution.

Our global counterparts have a vision to rebuild the credibility of the marketing profession by being held accountable for growth. Transparency was the first step, predicting business outcomes from media investments might just be the next.

In Australia, whatever we decide to do, or not, to address the global marketing growth agenda, we are going to be swept up in the international undercurrents. Better to swim than sink.

Sunita Gloster is a director of PricewaterhouseCoopers' CMO advisory.
